newsitem.title: USA: Sony unveils first U.S. high-definition TV line.
newsitem.headline: Sony unveils first U.S. high-definition TV line.

text.p: Sony Corp. Wednesday unveiled a full line of broadcast equipment for studio and field production of high-definition video programming, in a bid to accelerate the TV industry's conversion to digital production.

Sony officials said the products will be the first such professional-quality equipment introduced in the United States since the U.S. government settled on an industrywide standard for digital broadcasts late last year.

The products included high-definition cameras for use in studios, portable cameras for mobile news crews and a line of high-definition studio monitors and associated storage and networking equipment used in video editing and distribution.
High Definition Television (HDTV) is the emerging standard for a new generation of TVs that offer picture images twice as crisp and on larger screens than conventional TV.
The transition to HDTV -- often compared to the switch made to colour from black-and-white decades ago -- is expected to wow audiences and usher in a new era of TV viewing.
But promises of a digital TV future remain constrained by the absence of broadcast equipment to produce high-definition TV and consumer TV sets necessary to receive the programming.

Major manufacturers such as Sony, Toshiba Corp., Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. Ltd.'s Panasonic and Philips Electronics NV plan to have wide-screen HDTV sets on the market by early 1998, but it will take well into the next century before such sets replace existing models.
The Sony product line is designed to be sold as part of a complete studio production package allowing a TV station to shoot video, edit, store and transmit HDTV programming.

The consumer electronics giant's High Defintion Video System (HDVS) products run the pricing gamut, with cameras, for example, starting at about $70,000. Some of the equipment will be available as early as this spring with other HDVS products ready by the end of the year.

While a standard digital video production package for a small TV station typically costs about $500,000 to $1 million, an equivalent high-definition package will be priced about 20 percent to 30 percent more, said Charles Steinberg, presdident of Sony's U.S business and professional broadcasting unit.

TV broadcasters have moved hesitantly to embrace the new technology, fearing the massive investments involved in switching to high-definition digital TV from the older mix of analogue and digital equipment that now dominate TV studios.

The CBS and NBC networks have said they are planning to begin broadcasting in HDTV once they are awarded digital channels by federal regulators. The networks are expected to launch such services by late 1998.

Sony and other equipment makers have adopted a carrot-and-stick approach to woo broadcasters, offering hybrid equipment that allow TV networks and independent producers to create standard TV as well as HDTV-style programmming.

As a means of speeding the adoption of the new technology industrywide, Sony said it is making available to competitors the specialised computer chips it has developed to compress and decompress data-heavy HDTV signals.

Fear of being left behind by newer technologies like direct-to-home satellite broadcasters and Internet-based TV programmers is prodding the traditional TV networks to adopt the high-defenition technology or risk losing their audiences.

Also Wednesday, Sony said it had won a multimillion-dollar contract from Hughes Electronics Corp. and six Japanese companies to create a HDTV production facility for the new DirecTV operation in Japan.

It also said it is building a digital studio for Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. in Arizona as part of the global media power's thrust into the U.S. market with a satellite-to-home network called American Sky Broadcasting (ASkyB).
Sony's equipment will be on display at a broadcasting equipment trade show, the National Association of Broadcasters, which begins in Las Vegas on April 7.
